Evaluating the uncertainty of machine learning models is critical to gauge the credibility of their predictions. Despite this, several factors impact the accuracy of uncertainty assessments, one of which is the degree of model misspecification. Given that models inherently fall short of fully representing reality, we question whether uncertainty estimates under these conditions can be trusted. This paper posits that model misspecification warrants greater consideration, and we illustrate our point through theoretical scenarios and reference relevant academic work.

To efficiently explore the solution space in integer programming using branch-and-bound methods, we must determine the order in which to examine the next nodes, a problem known as node comparison. Our proposed siamese graph neural network model tackles this issue by representing nodes as bipartite graphs with attributes and trains the model to mimic the decision-making process of an expert algorithm that converges towards the optimal solution. Our model is evaluated on a standard framework that ranks nodes according to their score, and we demonstrate that it outperforms the default ranking function in the SCIP solver as well as competing machine learning methods on three challenging NP-hard benchmarks. Furthermore, we show that our approach generalizes well to larger problem instances than those used for training. The code for reproducing our experiments is available at https://github.com/ds4dm/learn2comparenodes.

We explore multi-agent Markov games with nonlinear function approximation, focusing on low-rank games with a hidden structure that combines a nonlinear representation. Our objective is to develop an efficient algorithm for discovering an approximate equilibrium policy without prior knowledge, suitable for deep learning implementation. By employing representation learning, we design model-based and model-free approaches to construct an effective representation from collected data. Both methods achieve polynomial sample complexity, which can degrade exponentially with the number of players in the worst case. To overcome this challenge, we introduce Markov games with a factorized transition structure and present an efficient algorithm for this scenario. Our result provides the first sample-efficient solution for multi-agent Markov games incorporating nonlinear function approximation. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm through a neural network-based implementation, outperforming the popular DQN with fictitious play method.

The Data Bricks Space Mission is an activity prototype centered on data physicalization aimed at teaching data concepts to children aged 10-12. Developed through a comprehensive literature review and consultation with elementary school teachers, this activity utilizes a narrative space adventure and Lego bricks to enable students to collect, analyze, and present data, fostering an appreciation for the connection between data and reality.

Predicting the orbits of objects in low Earth orbit is compromised by uncertainty in atmospheric density estimates, which is critical for tasks like satellite conjunction analysis and space situational awareness. This study investigates the impact of density uncertainties on orbit error propagation, using probabilistic machine learning models to represent these uncertainties. We employ the HASDM-ML, CHAMP-ML, and MSIS-UQ density estimation models to analyze the effects of density correlations on orbit uncertainty. Due to the complexity of density correlations, we develop multiple Monte Carlo methods and also utilize the Kalman filtering technique for orbit uncertainty propagation, but the latter is computationally faster. However, standard Kalman filter frameworks struggle to translate density uncertainties into orbital state uncertainties. To address this, we utilize the consider covariance sigma point filter, which can account for density uncertainties during orbit propagation. We validate our approach by comparing the CCSP filter with Monte Carlo methods and propose an ensemble approach for orbit uncertainty quantification under different space weather conditions using the HASDM-ML, CHAMP-ML, and MSIS-UQ density models.

Conventional cluster-robust standard errors lack robustness and can be easily compromised by data with a few extremely large clusters. In specific scenarios, such as using U.S. states as clusters, a large cluster can account for a significant portion of the total sample, violating the assumptions required for the cluster-robust methods to function. We demonstrate that these methods fail when cluster sizes adhere to a power law distribution with an exponent less than two, exemplified not only by the 51-state clusters but also by several real-world cases documented in prominent research papers. In response to these limitations of existing cluster-robust methods, we propose an alternative approach, a weighted cluster-robust (WCR) method that offers a straightforward solution. Our simulation studies validate the robustness of WCR and the vulnerability of conventional CR methods under certain conditions.

The difficulty in leveraging dynamic graphs for predictive tasks stems from extracting temporal patterns and motifs from constantly changing graphs, where task labels are often scarce, expensive, and unevenly distributed. Self-supervised learning has shown promise, particularly on static graphs, yet current approaches to dynamic graphs struggle with forecasting interactions beyond short-term horizons. To address these limitations, we introduce DyG2Vec, a self-supervised model for dynamic graph representation learning, which uses a window-based approach to generate node embeddings for future interaction forecasting. In contrast to existing models, DyG2Vec achieves superior performance on benchmark datasets while requiring significantly less training and inference time. Furthermore, we adapt self-supervised learning evaluation mechanisms to accommodate dynamic graphs, demonstrating that pre-training with SSL can lead to more robust and reliable temporal node representations, especially in scenarios with limited labels.

Building on earlier research, Gelfand and MacPherson in 1992 established a local and combinatorial framework for calculating the Pontrjagin classes of a differential manifold, which we further elaborate upon in this context, tracing their contributions to the emergence of combinatorial differential manifolds.

Recent breakthroughs in the study of fission fragment angular momentum have generated significant attention and research focus. The concurrent measurement of neutrons and gamma rays in association with fission fragments continues to be the most crucial technique in the investigation of fission physics. In pursuit of these objectives, we have created an innovative system consisting of a cutting-edge fission fragment sensor and neutron-gamma radiation detectors. A novel, twin Frisch-gridded ionization chamber has been designed and manufactured, specifically suited for use with a natural spontaneous fission source alongside a 40-module array of organic scintillators at the Argonne National Laboratory. The new ionization chamber design seeks to minimize particle loss through its walls, resulting in a compact, self-contained system compatible with existing experimental frameworks. The chamber can accurately measure fission fragment properties such as mass and kinetic energy, whereas the organic scintillators can detect neutron and gamma-ray activity. This setup is further detailed, along with initial experimental findings and the prospects of future event-by-event analysis and experiments.

A theoretical model of neutron star spontaneous scalarization developed by Damour and Esposito-Farese suggests that a general relativistic branch becomes unstable, triggering rapid growth of a scalar field, resulting in a scalarized branch. This model, applied to cosmology, reveals an unstable scalar field during the inflationary and matter-dominated epochs, which conflicts with solar system constraints on today's scalar field value. In a scenario proposed by Anson et al., a four-point interaction between the scalar field and an inflaton field, along with a mass term heavier than the Hubble scale, can suppress the scalar field during inflation, thus allowing it to remain small despite growth in the radiation-dominated epoch. This study investigates the dynamics of the scalar field during reheating and other cosmological epochs for various inflaton potentials. It was found that for a certain range of coupling values, the scalar field can be amplified by parametric resonance during coherent inflaton oscillations, but incorporating the backreaction of created particles yields significantly lower maximum scalar field values during preheating. Furthermore, the minimum coupling values compatible with solar system constraints on the scalar field value at the end of reheating are approximately 10 to the power of negative 5, indicating a broad range of acceptable coupling values. This outcome naturally leads to viable cosmological evolution of the scalar field, consistent with local gravity constraints, without altering the properties of scalarized neutron stars.

Classification of objects from LiDAR 3D point cloud data is crucial in modern applications, such as autonomous driving. Nonetheless, labeling these point clouds requires significant human effort due to their complex 3D nature. This paper introduces a semi-supervised learning strategy, where we rely on 3D object models to train classifiers without relying on manually annotated point clouds, achieving performance comparable to fully-supervised methods. We simulate real-world point clouds by sampling 3D models from various viewpoints and angles of partial occlusion. We then create more realistic point clouds through random rotations and adding noise, and train point cloud encoding models, such as DGCNN and PointNet++, on these augmented datasets. The resulting classifiers are evaluated for their ability to generalize to real-world datasets. We also present a new benchmark, called Point-Syn2Real, which evaluates cross-domain learning performance on point clouds. Extensive experiments on this dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach in achieving superior cross-domain generalizability in both indoor and outdoor settings, surpassing existing methods. The code and dataset will be available upon publication.

This paper showcases novel assaults on federated learning when applied to
train language text models. We test the attacks' effectiveness against a
popular model from Google's GBoard app, a pioneering example of production
federated learning. We find that an adversary can accurately recover text
messages typed on a user's mobile device, regardless of conditions, and that
countermeasures like mini-batches and local noise addition are ineffective.
Moreover, we demonstrate that sentence structure can be precisely
reconstructed, posing significant privacy risks given GBoard's live
deployment.

In 2019, researchers constructed a pair of Banach space operators that are equivalent after extension but not Schur coupled, addressing a decades-long question posed by Bart and Tsekanovskii. These operators, defined on incomparable Banach spaces, have the same Fredholm index but different properties in relation to operator equivalence and Schur coupling. The present study investigates these relationships further, revealing a surprising dichotomy: for Fredholm operators of a fixed index, being Schur coupled is equivalent to being equivalent after extension only when certain geometric conditions on the Banach spaces are met. To explore this phenomenon, we introduce two numerical indices that reflect the coincidence or disparity between these two operator properties and demonstrate their connection to the geometric characteristics of the Banach spaces involved, using examples of exotic Banach spaces constructed by Gowers and Maurey as well as subsequent work by Aiena, Gonzalez, and Ferenczi.

We have established novel limitations on galaxy formation physics at a redshift of z greater than or equal to 7 for Eridanus II, a low-mass, local ultra-faint dwarf galaxy. By applying a one-zone chemical evolution model to Eridanus II's photometric metallicity distribution, we find that its evolution is consistent with a short, exponentially declining star formation history, a low star formation efficiency, and a significant mass loading factor. These results suggest that Eridanus II formed most of its stars before the end of the reionization era and support the presence of strong outflows in the galaxy. Additionally, our findings indicate that nearly all the metals produced in Eridanus II were ejected. Future studies can verify these predictions by analyzing the distribution of magnesium to iron ratios and the presence of extremely metal-poor stars. Further research, specifically the analysis of Eridanus II's highest metallicity stars, will refine our understanding of the galaxy's evolution.

The distribution of atomic hydrogen within galaxies at various points in time is represented by the neutral atomic hydrogen mass function, offering valuable insights into galaxy formation models. By analyzing 21cm spectroscopy data from the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope focused on blue star-forming galaxies between redshifts 0.20 and 0.42, we have established a correlation between average atomic hydrogen mass and absolute B-band magnitude at a redshift of 0.35. Combining this correlation with known luminosity functions, we have estimated the atomic hydrogen mass function at the specified redshift and found that the correct scatter in this correlation is crucial for achieving an accurate estimate. The atomic hydrogen mass function has undergone significant changes between redshifts 0.35 and 0, particularly in high-mass galaxies, which have a lower prevalence at the earlier time point. Conversely, the abundance of low-mass galaxies at this earlier time point is higher compared to the present. Although our results may be influenced by cosmic variance, we conclude that massive star-forming galaxies have accumulated a considerable amount of atomic hydrogen through mergers or the acquisition of surrounding gas over the past four Gyr.

This article deals with one-dimensional dispersive flows that exhibit cubic nonlinearities on the real line, focusing on the focusing case where initial data may contain small solitons. A recent conjecture proposed global, scattering solutions for defocusing flows with small initial data, and it was proven that global solutions for such flows satisfy certain estimates. In contrast, the focusing scenario presents challenges, and we instead explore the existence of long-time solutions and their behavior over time. Our main finding, applicable to both Schrödinger dispersion relations and general cases, demonstrates that solutions exist for a duration of approximately $\epsilon^{-8}$ and meet the desired estimates for up to $\epsilon^{-6}$. This achievement represents a milestone in reaching a previously unknown threshold.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares have been documented through precise photometry from space missions like Kepler and TESS. This data is crucial for analyzing the habitability of planets around low-mass stars. However, these assessments rely heavily on incomplete observations, particularly the lack of near-ultraviolet light data during stellar flares. Researchers have utilized detailed simulations to predict the near-ultraviolet light emitted during a massive flare on the star AD Leo. By combining high-energy electron beam simulations with lower-energy simulations, scientists were able to explain various aspects of the flare, such as the broadening of hydrogen lines and the changes in optical light. By analyzing data from solar flares and applying it to the simulation results, researchers have interpreted the findings as the superposition of bright, high-energy flare centers and fainter, larger-scale flares.

The motion of a coupled system consisting of a physical pendulum filled with a compressible viscous fluid is investigated. It's found that the fluid's presence significantly affects the pendulum's movement. Specifically, under certain conditions, the fluid behaves as a damper, leading the system to eventually reach a state of rest. This rest state is characterized by a static density distribution of the fluid and the pendulum's center of mass in equilibrium. These results, proven for a broad class of weak solutions, apply to any initial conditions with finite energy. Additional numerical simulations demonstrate that higher fluid compressibility accelerates this process, allowing the system to rest much faster.

Countable locally standard measure algebras can be represented by pairs consisting of a Steinitz number and a real number of at least 1, mirroring the theorems established by J. Dixmier and A.A. Baranov.

Recommender systems encounter significant challenges when a new user registers on the platform or a novel item is introduced to the product line. To address this item cold-start issue, we recommend substituting the conventional embedding layer in sequential recommenders with a dynamic data storage system that doesn't require learnable parameters and can accommodate a virtually limitless number of representations. In our research, we introduce FELRec, a sophisticated embedding network capable of iteratively refining the existing representations of users and items as new data becomes available. Unlike comparable approaches, our proposed model effectively represents new users and items without the need for supplementary information or time-consuming retraining. In comparison to similar methodologies, FELRec demonstrates improved performance by 29.50%-47.45% during item cold-start situations. Additionally, our model exhibits excellent generalizability to unseen datasets. The source code for our proposed model is freely accessible at github.com/kweimann/FELRec.

Modularizing the text-only adaptation of a transducer model for end-to-end speech recognition poses significant challenges. Since the transducer lacks distinct components for acoustic models, language models, or blank models, we introduce a hybrid autoregressive transducer called MHAT that integrates separate decoders for labels and blanks, along with a shared acoustic encoder. MHAT's structure enables direct projections to acoustic models and internal language models, allowing the computation of label posteriors. Our training process combines an internal language model loss and a hybrid autoregressive transducer loss, ensuring the MHAT's internal language model can be adapted independently for effective text adaptation. MHAT's ability to adapt to text has been found to improve language model fusion, resulting in significant reductions in word error rates when applied to large-scale production data.

Researchers have employed complex learning models to develop approximate solutions to NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, including vertex classification in graphs to identify optimal sets. By leveraging a learning framework, we have optimized a pruning process for the maximum clique enumeration problem, reducing its runtime. Our investigation into the impact of various vertex representations on this heuristic method reveals the effectiveness of graph embedding algorithms like Node2vec and DeepWalk in facilitating node classification. Moreover, combining local graph features with feature elimination yields more accurate results, demonstrating the potential of this approach. We have validated the robustness and scalability of our method through experiments on randomly generated graphs.

This research explores the behavior of high-frequency waves within highly-dispersive media that exhibit nonlinear absorption. Building on foundational methods like the Wigner transform and multiscale analysis, we establish a set of semilinear radiative transport models for the phase-space intensity and the corresponding diffusive approximations. We further examine an inverse problem related to the semilinear transport equation, focusing on recovering the absorption coefficients based on a specific function of the equation's solution, and we demonstrate the uniqueness of the recovery result.

The life-threatening skin condition, melanoma, is caused by an abnormal growth of melanocytes in human skin and can be treated with early diagnosis, facilitated by the segmentation of skin lesions in medical images. Several Fully Convolutional Network (FCN) models, including the U-Net architecture, have shown superior performance in segmentation tasks. However, these models are restricted by the locality of convolutional operations, limiting their ability to capture long-range dependencies essential for accurate segmentation. A recent approach has combined U-Net with Swin Transformer modules to achieve both local and global representations. Building on this concept, this paper proposes Att-SwinU-Net, a novel attention-based Swin U-Net extension designed to improve feature re-usability by optimizing the skip connection path through the incorporation of an attention mechanism. The proposed model has been validated through an extensive ablation study on various skin lesion segmentation datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness.

Structural investigations under extreme pressure conditions were conducted on CeBeH$_8$ and CeBH$_8$.  At a pressure of 10 GPa, $Fm\overline{3}m$-CeBeH$_8$ was found to exhibit superconductivity with a transition temperature of 56 K. Similar phase transitions occurred in CeBH$_8$ but required higher pressure and resulted in increased superconducting transition temperatures. Our calculations predict $Fm\overline{3}m$-CeBH$_8$ to exhibit superconductivity above 120 GPa, reaching a maximum transition temperature of 118 K at 150 GPa. Additionally, $R\overline{3}m$-CeBH$_8$ and $C2/m$-CeBH$_8$ were found to remain dynamically stable above 120 GPa and 100 GPa, respectively, and achieved maximum transition temperatures of 123 K and 115 K at pressures of 195 GPa and 350 GPa, respectively. Our study broadens the range of ternary hydrides and may guide further searches for superconducting hydrides at low to moderate pressures.

The movement of biological molecules across cell membranes is crucial for cellular functions and has been explored in this research by simulating the passage of polymers through a tapered channel, from its widest point to its narrowest end. Employing molecular dynamics, the study examines how the geometry of the conical pore and the length of the polymers influence the translocation process. Specifically, the researchers investigated the total time required for translocation, the probability of polymer segments escaping the narrow end of the channel, and the effect of pore asymmetry on translocation dynamics. Notably, the findings indicate significant differences between translocation processes that begin at either end of the conical channel, in accordance with existing experimental data. The investigation has also considered the impact of polymer rigidity and increasing chain length on both types of translocation processes, providing insights into the transition from direction-dependent to direction-independent translocation through an asymmetric channel.

Agricultural precision seeks to boost crop yields through the strategic application of technological advancements, while minimizing expenses and conserving resources within the agricultural industry. Our research draws on nature, specifically the visual capabilities of bees, to develop a cutting-edge remote sensing system capable of incorporating UV reflectance in identifying flowers. This system enables the creation of high-quality images that can be utilized in conjunction with deep learning to detect strawberry flowers accurately. Furthermore, we integrate our UV-based flower detection system into a cost-efficient and scalable aerial monitoring robotic platform, and compare its effectiveness with a comparable method utilizing standard RGB images.

Our research combines the EUropean Heliospheric FORcasting Information Asset (EUHFORIA) model and the improved Particle Acceleration and Transport in the Heliosphere (iPATH) model to simulate the large solar energetic particle event on November 29, 2020. We compared the simulated time-intensity profiles to measurements at Parker Solar Probe, STEREO-A, SOlar and Heliospheric Observatory, and Solar Orbiter. We explored the effect of past shock acceleration on the SEP time-intensity profiles and investigated the root cause of this widespread SEP event. Our analysis of shock parameters and particle fluxes during the event revealed that a realistic solar wind background can significantly affect shock expansion and, consequently, shock characteristics. Our simulation accurately reproduced time-intensity profiles with an energetic storm particle event at Parker Solar Probe, and simulated and observed time-intensity profiles of protons showed a similar two-phase enhancement at STA. Our results highlight the importance of modelling a shock using a realistic solar wind in determining SEP event characteristics. Additionally, our model's time-intensity profiles at Earth decay phase agreed well with observations, emphasizing the significance of perpendicular diffusion in widespread SEP events. Accounting for the possible large curved magnetic field line connecting to Solar Orbiter, our model's time-intensity profiles showed good agreement with observations, suggesting that the largely distorted magnetic field lines due to a stream interaction region may be key to understanding the observed SEPs at Solar Orbiter in this event.

This research explores the concept of personalized dose adjustment using Bayesian optimization to tailor optimal medication doses to each individual, ultimately enhancing treatment efficacy.  The method of interior point optimization ensures patient safety with a high degree of confidence, which is illustrated through a real-world scenario where patients with type 1 diabetes can find the ideal bolus insulin dose to mitigate the effects of meals.  By commencing with no prior knowledge about the patients, our proposed algorithm is capable of achieving improved therapeutic results, measured by the percentage of time spent within a target range, without compromising patient safety.  Additionally, potential future healthcare applications of this technology are also examined.

Point cloud data has become a staple in many scientific disciplines. Recent advances in geometric deep learning have led to its widespread adoption for prediction tasks, but these models can be complex and challenging to interpret, making it difficult for researchers to apply them in their work. To address this limitation, a new approach called learnable randomness injection has been developed, which enables the creation of inherently interpretable models based on existing geometric deep learning frameworks. These models can pinpoint the specific data points in point cloud data that are most relevant to predicting the target outcome. Furthermore, a set of real-world datasets spanning high-energy physics and biochemistry has been created to test the effectiveness of this approach, demonstrating its ability to produce more accurate and consistent results than existing methods. The proposed mechanism is underpinned by the information bottleneck principle and has been found to yield models that are more resilient to shifts in the data distribution. The code and datasets used in this research are available for download at a GitHub repository.

This paper introduces the Value Iteration Network for Reward Shaping (VIN-RS), a novel reward shaping mechanism utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The proposed VIN-RS incorporates a CNN trained with computed labels via the message passing mechanism of Hidden Markov Models. By leveraging CNNs and message passing, VIN-RS can accurately predict shaping values from images or graphs of the environment. Current research on reward shaping faces challenges in learning MDP representations and estimating transition matrices. VIN-RS overcomes these limitations by constructing a potential function from an estimated MDP and automatically inferring the environment's transition matrix. VIN-RS achieves this by estimating the transition matrix using self-learned convolution filters and extracting environmental details from input frames or graphs. Building upon previous successes with message passing and CNN planning behavior, the proposed VIN-RS utilizes these messages to train its CNN. Evaluations on tabular games, Atari 2600, and MuJoCo demonstrate the effectiveness of VIN-RS, resulting in improved learning speed and maximum cumulative rewards compared to existing approaches.

Segerman's 15+4 puzzle offers a hinged variation of the classic 15-puzzle where tiles can pivot as they shift, mirroring Wilson's 1974 work on classifying sliding block puzzle solutions. We extend Wilson's findings to puzzles like the 15+4, where tiles can rotate, revealing that their solution sets correspond to subgroups of generalized symmetric groups. With the exception of two distinct scenarios, our analysis reveals that the solution group of such a puzzle either encompasses the entire generalized symmetric group or falls into one of two smaller, index-two subgroups.
This paper counters some proposed statements by Marques and Lengyel regarding $p$-adic valuation in Tribonacci sequence members.

Advanced technologies such as particle tracking velocimetry have been pivotal in deciphering the intricate nature of three-dimensional turbulent flows, which are prevalent in both natural and industrial environments. Despite the progress in 3D data acquisition, existing particle tracking algorithms face significant challenges, including handling large particle movements, dense particle distributions, and computationally intensive processes. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel end-to-end solution based on a deep neural network called GotFlow3D, which employs recurrent Graph Optimal Transport. This innovative network creates two graphs in geometric and feature spaces and enhances particle representations by incorporating intrinsic and extrinsic features learned from a graph neural network. By extracting and processing deep features, GotFlow3D determines optimal transport plans that identify particle pair correspondences, which are iteratively retrieved to guide recurrent flow learning. Evaluations of GotFlow3D on both numerical simulations and real-world experiments demonstrate its superiority over recent scene flow learners and particle tracking algorithms, boasting remarkable accuracy, robustness, and generalization capabilities. These findings offer valuable insights into the intricate dynamics of diverse physical and biological systems.

Exceptional points, which are also referred to as defective spectral degeneracy, play a crucial role in various unusual phenomena in fields like optics, acoustics, and other systems that don't follow conservative rules. Despite extensive research over the past twenty years, the interactions of multiple exceptional points or lines and the rules that govern these interactions have been poorly understood. This paper presents a general rule for understanding how multiple exceptional points behave together in complex systems, which are non-Hermitian, and reveals some unexpected effects. We demonstrate that two exceptional points with opposite charges do not always annihilate each other when they approach, depending on how they get close to each other. Furthermore, our research finds that the rule imposes strict constraints on what forms these exceptional lines can take, excluding some configurations like the Hopf link but permitting novel ring structures made up of lines that don't follow the usual rules. These effects can be demonstrated in models that can be easily implemented in platforms like acoustic cavities, optical waveguides, and ring resonators, which can lay the foundation for a deeper understanding of the non-Abelian exceptional topology and provide insights into how to use these effects for a wide range of manipulations and applications.

Malfunctions in electrical distribution networks pose a significant threat to
safety and infrastructure. High Impedance Faults (HIF) are hazardous yet difficult
to identify due to low fault currents and their complex behavior. In New Zealand,
large-scale distribution networks lack extensive monitoring, making HIF detection a
research priority. A test facility has been constructed to analyze power system
faults and develop a fault detection system. By simulating various faults and
analyzing the data, a deep learning classifier was trained to recognize HIF from
its distinct signature. An outdoor sensing system has been developed and installed
in Wellington Electricity's network to gather further data and evaluate the
technology. This paper focuses on the results of experiments involving tree
branches, as they exhibited the most extensive range of HIF phenomena. A sensing
system has been mounted on a pole in Wellington Electricity's network, with
outcomes from the installation yet to be reported in full.

Optimizing the transportation of ore from mines to ports is crucial for mining supply chains, which are often plagued by increasing costs and limited resources.  Large-scale mining companies seek to efficiently allocate their resources to minimize operational costs.  Past research has investigated this challenge under the title of resource-constrained job scheduling (RCJS).  While various optimization techniques have been developed to address the deterministic version, the inherent uncertainty surrounding resource availability in mining operations has received relatively little attention.  RCJS with uncertainty is a complex problem that cannot be effectively solved with existing optimization methods.  This study introduces an adaptive simulated annealing algorithm that overcomes the limitations of current approaches to RCJS with uncertainty, including premature convergence, excessive hyper-parameters, and inefficiency in handling diverse uncertainty levels.  The proposed algorithm achieves a balance between exploration and exploitation through the use of a population, modified cooling schedule, and adaptive mechanism for selecting perturbation operators.  Results indicate that the new algorithm outperforms existing methods across a range of benchmark RCJS instances and uncertainty levels, discovering new best-known solutions for nearly all problem instances.

A fundamental challenge in modern physics is determining whether gravity operates classically or quantum mechanically in controlled laboratory settings. Researchers have suggested an approach to verify the quantum nature of gravity by creating quantum superpositions of two close but distinct neutral masses. However, preparing the lighter mass in a superposition state requires proximity to equipment that itself constitutes a heavier quantum system. Given gravity's universal influence, this heavier system could naturally cause decoherence in the lighter mass. This paper explores the conditions under which entanglement between the two lighter masses can persist despite decoherence caused by the heavier systems, using pairs of light and heavy quantum oscillators as test models. Ultimately, it provides an estimation of the level of decoherence in the proposed experiment designed to test the quantum aspects of gravity.

Breaking away from the confines of a single language and mode of interaction, researchers have started to combine language technologies with multiple modalities and languages. While progress has been made in individual areas, research on multimodal and multilingual language technologies has largely focused on English and text-based contexts respectively. To address this limitation, researchers have taken a holistic approach to integrating multiple languages and modalities, known as MultiX, and aimed to categorize and characterize the resulting tasks, datasets, and methods. In doing so, they have examined various languages, dataset types, and annotation schemes, as well as how languages and modalities interact within models. The study also explores the advantages and disadvantages of different modeling approaches to determine their reliability in specific scenarios. The investigation ultimately aims to reveal the overarching trends in the field and provide a roadmap for future research directions and challenges.

Currently, the Milky Way is undergoing a major merger. A dwarf galaxy, similar to the Sagittarius dwarf spheroidal galaxy, is experiencing tidal destruction as it orbits the Milky Way. Its close passes around the galaxy are disturbing the Milky Way's disc. Through a series of hydrodynamical simulations, this work explores the effects of massive dwarf galaxies on star formation within Milky Way-like discs, with a focus on quasi-polar orbits similar to the Sagittarius dwarf. We have confirmed that interactions between a host galaxy and orbiting satellites can enhance star formation within the host. In cases of close passes (<20 kpc) between massive (>2 \times 10^10 Msun) gas-poor satellites and the host, significant short-term star formation bursts are observed. For gas-rich satellites, we have found that while star formation is enhanced over longer timescales, there are no prominent peaks in the star formation history. Instead, gas is steadily stripped from the satellite and transferred to the host, smoothing the star formation rate variations. We have determined that the impact of satellite perturbations is primarily observed in the outer (>10 kpc) disc of the host. Furthermore, the close passes of satellites have resulted in the creation of a substantial amount of low-metallicity stars in the host, with the most pronounced effect occurring when satellites transfer gas and dilute the mean stellar metallicity after the first pericentric passage of massive satellites. Our simulations suggest that the recent passages of the Sagittarius galaxy are responsible for the star formation bursts observed in the solar neighbourhood (\approx 1 and \approx 2 Gyr ago); however, to replicate the initial star formation burst (\approx 6 Gyr ago), we require a close pericentric passage (<20 kpc) and significant mass loss from the Sagittarius precursor.

Research into the antiferromagnetism and chiral-d wave superconductivity on a honeycomb lattice near an antiferromagnetic Mott state at half band filling is conducted using a t-J model and slave boson mean field theory. The order parameters and single particle energy spectra at various band filling levels are examined. The results show that antiferromagnetism boosts superconductivity and results in nodal single particle energy spectra at two band filling levels, which is an unusual finding given the nodeless chiral-d wave superconducting order typically expected. The investigation also compares antiferromagnetic chiral-d wave states with antiferromagnetic extended-s wave states, highlighting key features of chiral-d wave superconducting states. The findings of this study may be applicable to honeycomb lattice materials, such as the In$_3$Cu$_2$VO$_9$ compound.

We analyze mathematical equations modeling electrostatic MEMS systems. The equations, which involve specific functions and a parameter, are given by: 

$\varphi\big(r,u'(r)\big) = \lambda\int_0^r\frac{f(s)}{g(u(s))}\,\mathrm{d}s$, $0 < r < 1$, $0 < u(r) < 1$ and $u(1) = 0$. Our work focuses on proving the existence of solutions, their regularity and determining the range of voltages at which the devices collapse. In a specific case, where the functions take the form $\varphi(r,v) = r^\alpha |v|^\beta v$, we derive the exact asymptotic behavior of solutions near the origin.

A technique called neutron imaging offers non-destructive inspection capabilities across a wide variety of fields, but achieving high spatial resolution is crucial and poses a significant challenge. A promising approach involves developing a neutron detector with a high resolution using fine-grained nuclear emulsion. In order to improve image quality, it's necessary to have a high track density, but current analysis methods struggle with this. Through simulations, it was discovered that an average of 10,000 tracks per 100 by 100 square micrometers is sufficient for neutron imaging. Further research involved examining image contrast across various track densities and neutron transmission rates. Experimentation with gadolinium-based gratings with well-known structures also led to successful imaging results. Measurements of the 1 sigma 10-90 percent edge response, using grayscale images of the grating slits with a 9-micrometer periodic structure, yielded a value of 0.945 plus or minus 0.004 micrometers.

In 6G cellular networks, Joint Communication and Sensing (JCAS) is pivotal, with detecting the operating environment, especially when humans are present, being equally important as high-speed wireless connectivity. To circumvent signal blockage, an initial step involves sensing and identifying types of blockage. To this end, we investigate the feasibility of using human movement detection as a proxy task for identifying blockage types through experiments validating hypotheses, utilizing both qualitative assessment via visual inspection and quantitative evaluation through hyperparameter tuning of deep learning models. This approach is advantageous for testing and pre-training deep learning models, necessitating a minimal amount of data from the actual JCAS environment. Consequently, a small dataset is collected from a 26 GHz multi-user communication device with hybrid beamforming. The data is transformed into Doppler Frequency Spectrum and utilized for hypothesis validation. Our research demonstrates that (i) domain shift between learning and inference data necessitates the use of deep learning models that can effectively handle it, (ii) input data dilution to increase dataset size should be avoided, (iii) a small volume of input data is insufficient for reasonable inference performance, (iv) higher sensing resolution should be managed by performing more actions/gestures per frame and decreasing the sampling rate, and (v) a higher reported sampling rate during pre-processing may enhance performance but should be individually tested on a per task basis.

In numerous real-world applications such as marketing campaigns, loan management, and e-commerce, assigning items to their respective owners is a widespread issue. This assignment problem, given specific objectives and numerous constraints, can be formulated as a constrained optimization problem, which is typically NP-hard, especially when dealing with large numbers of items or owners. Given the magnitude of items in this case, reaching exact solutions is nearly impossible. This study focuses on solving constrained assignment problems involving hundreds of millions of items and tens of owners, a scale commonly seen in the internet industry. By relaxing the integer constraint and formulating a generalized optimization problem, its objective function becomes convex, and its constraints become linear or separable by items. This generalized problem can be effectively solved within the Bregman Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (BADMM) framework, where Bregman divergence is leveraged to transform the Augmented Lagrangian into a separable form. This separation enables the solving of multiple subproblems in parallel and can be implemented using a MapReduce-style distributed computation framework. Experiment results on both synthetic and real-world datasets are presented to verify its accuracy and scalability.

We've developed new algorithms for wireless image transmission over Rayleigh fading MIMO channels, utilizing channel state information at the receiver. Two transmission strategies are considered, one leveraging spatial diversity and the other spatial multiplexing. The diversity scheme employs an orthogonal space-time block code to maximize robustness against channel fluctuations. In contrast, the multiplexing scheme enables direct mapping of codewords to antennas, utilizing additional freedom to convey source information. Our simulations indicate that the diversity scheme outperforms the multiplexing scheme at lower signal-to-noise ratios and with fewer receive antennas, yet loses benefits when the number of transmit antennas exceeds two. Moreover, both schemes can match the performance of the state-of-the-art BPG algorithm at MIMO capacity in the examined scenarios.

This research introduces a novel replica exchange preconditioned Langevin diffusion approach, referred to as repCNLD, to efficiently handle complex distributions with multiple modes and high-dimensional parameters. Addressing high-dimensional distribution sampling remains a pressing issue, with conventional MCMC methods often losing efficacy as parameter dimensions increase. Many MCMC algorithms struggle to capture all modes of a distribution when the energy function is not convex. In contrast, repCNLD accelerates the convergence of pCNLD by leveraging the robust Crank-Nicolson discretization method. Notably, the proposed repCNLD exhibits linear growth in discretization error relative to the time step size. To further enhance efficiency, repCNLD is extended to a multi-variance setting, enabling accelerated convergence and reduced computational costs. An unbiased estimator of the swapping rate for multi-variance repCNLD is derived, providing a basis for selecting a suitable low-fidelity model for the second chain. Performance evaluations are conducted on high-dimensional Gaussian mixture models and nonlinear PDE inverse problems, with the latter leveraging the discrete adjoint method to efficiently compute gradients.

A common method for analyzing whole-slide images using WSI-level annotations is Multiple Instance Learning (MIL), which divides WSIs into patches to reduce computational costs and memory usage. To address the limitations of MIL, a novel framework called EmbAugmenter has been developed. This data augmentation technique uses a generative adversarial network to create synthetic augmentations directly within the embedding space, rather than in pixel space. The results of applying EmbAugmenter to the SICAPv2 dataset demonstrate that it outperforms MIL without augmentation and is comparable to traditional patch-level augmentation, while significantly reducing the training time.

This section provides a comprehensive update on the latest findings regarding CP violation and mixing in $B$ meson decay research. By examining the decays of $B^0_d$ into $J/\psi K^0_S$ and $B^0_s$ into $J/\psi \phi$, we aim to determine the mixing phases $\phi_d$ and $\phi_s$, incorporating hadronic uncertainties through the utilization of available data. Notably, anomalies in non-leptonic decays, such as $B \to \pi K$ and $B^0_s \to D_s^{\mp} K^{\pm}$, are observed to exhibit intriguing patterns, potentially hinting at the presence of New Physics.

This text outlines efficient techniques for extracting specific permutations, including derangements and ménage arrangements. By providing algorithms to extract the kth permutation from a pre-sorted list in lexicographic order, these techniques aim to streamline this process. The approach involves a step-by-step breakdown of this problem, initially converting it into a related problem of counting permutations based on specific prefixes, ultimately employing rook theory as a solution. The applications of these techniques span across combinatorics, probability, statistics, and modeling disciplines.

By incorporating graph structure, Graph Neural Networks transcend basic Neural Networks, leveraging relational inductive bias, as opposed to treating nodes as randomly independent elements. Despite the expectation that GNNs will excel in real-world tasks, instances exist where GNNs either underperform or offer minimal improvement compared to graph-agnostic NNs. To pinpoint these situations, using the frameworks of graph signal processing and statistical hypothesis testing, two analytical metrics are introduced to determine when edge biases in features and labels fail to yield advantages. These metrics enable the assignment of a threshold value, allowing for the prediction of potential performance benefits that graph-aware models might hold over graph-agnostic models.

Our proposed method, the first of its kind for character-level white-box attacks on transformer models, relies on the observation that transformer models process words as subtokens and that replacing subtokens has a similar effect to altering individual characters. Our method consists of three key steps: we utilize a gradient-based approach to identify the most susceptible words in a sentence, then replace the original subtokens with new ones while maintaining the sentence's structure. We incorporate an adversarial loss to guide the replacement of subtokens and leverage the Gumbel-softmax trick to facilitate gradient propagation. To minimize character modifications, we impose visual and length constraints during the optimization process. Our method demonstrates superiority over previous attack methods in terms of success rate and edit distance through extensive experiments on sentence-level and token-level tasks. Moreover, human evaluations confirm that our generated adversarial examples retain their original labels.

The remnants of supernovae release energy back into their surroundings in the interstellar medium, a gas composed of multiple phases. In the shock-heated gas, warm molecular hydrogen plays a significant role in the cooling process. Recent studies have utilized the near-infrared emission lines of molecular hydrogen to investigate this phenomenon, but these studies were often limited by their narrow filter imaging or sparse, low-resolution mid-infrared spectroscopic observations. Our team has conducted near-infrared spectroscopic observations of the A, B, C, and G regions of the supernova remnant IC 443 using the K-band Multi-Object Spectrograph onboard the VLT. These observations have led to the detection of 20 H$_2$ ro-vibrational transitions, an H line, and two [Fe II] lines. The distribution of molecular hydrogen in these regions appears clumpy, with a range of scales from 0.1 to 0.008 pc. Our data indicate that the excitation temperature of the warm gas is between 1500 K and 2500 K. Moreover, our multi-phase analysis reveals stratified shock structures in all regions, providing an explanation for the coexistence of various shock types. Our findings have also allowed us to confirm or disprove previously identified young stellar objects in these regions, ultimately casting doubt on the proposal of triggered star formation caused by supernova remnant shocks in IC 443.

To accelerate neural network training and lower power consumption, researchers use data quantization. However, achieving this through low-bit quantized training is complicated, as equal-precision methods can cause significant accuracy losses, while existing mixed-precision methods struggle with optimal bit-width assignment. To address this challenge, a novel framework called DYNASTY is introduced. DYNASTY leverages fast online data analysis to identify sensitive areas and utilizes an adaptive bit-width mapping system to ensure stable training convergence. Experimental results on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet datasets show that DYNASTY can significantly speed up training, reducing energy consumption by up to $5.1$ times and $4.7$ times without compromising model accuracy, and with minimal hardware modifications.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a leading approach for achieving quantum advantage on near-term quantum computers, however, its reliability is often hindered by high device error rates when dealing with large numbers of qubits. In QAOA, each edge of a problem graph corresponds to a series of error-prone CNOT operations that significantly impacts the circuit's fidelity. Observing that real-world graphs often adhere to a power-law distribution with hotspot nodes, researchers developed the "FrozenQubits" method that freezes these nodes and divides the problem space into smaller, independent sub-spaces. This allows the resulting QAOA sub-circuits to be less susceptible to gate and decoherence errors due to reduced CNOT operations. Unlike previous approaches, FrozenQubits eliminates the need for computationally intensive post-processing. Results from evaluating over 5,300 QAOA circuits across eight IBM quantum computers demonstrate that FrozenQubits can improve solution quality by an average of 8.73x (and up to 57x), albeit with a 2x increase in required quantum resources.

A key question is how we can explain matter's behavior. Some theories rely on natural laws, the structure of space, or even the spacetime fabric itself for explanations, but these approaches have been criticized as being too speculative. In response, some propose reversing the explanation to prioritize dynamics, treating natural laws as codifying patterns in matter's behavior, and geometric structures as reflecting certain regularities. A similar approach is now being developed for spacetime, where the fabric itself is seen as an abstraction from matter's dynamics. This work lays the groundwork for analyzing and comparing various spacetime settings across different theories, essentially competing between spacetime descriptions to see which best aligns with the theory's underlying dynamics and kinematics.

The challenge of inducing bilingual lexicons with limited bilingual supervision is pivotal in multilingual NLP, with current state-of-the-art approaches leveraging cross-lingual word embeddings to capture cross-lingual word similarities. Existing solutions to this challenge rely on static word mapping (VecMap) or type-level embeddings extracted from multilingual pre-trained models, or a combination of these methods. We introduce BLICEr, a novel semi-supervised post-hoc reranking method that enhances cross-lingual word embedding capabilities for any precalculated CLWE space. The core idea involves extracting lexical knowledge from multilingual pre-trained models and combining it with original embeddings through three stages: 1) generating a word similarity dataset using positive and hard negative pairs, 2) fine-tuning the pre-trained model in a cross-encoder setup to predict similarity scores, and 3) combining original CLWE similarity scores with the BLI-tuned cross-encoder's score. BLICEr surpasses state-of-the-art results on diverse benchmarks, outperforming a range of strong baselines across various languages. We also test BLICEr's robustness across different CLWEs, yielding impressive results.

Images and their corresponding ground truth annotations for diagnosing unusual medical conditions are in short supply due to the rarity of affected patients and the limited expertise required for image annotation. As a result, conventional training methods for classifying images of skin lesions and similar conditions are often ineffective, particularly in cases where class distributions are skewed towards the rarest conditions. Meta-learning techniques, such as few-shot learning, aim to mitigate these challenges by achieving good results even with limited data. This paper focuses on improving meta-learning for classifying dermoscopic images by developing a baseline supervised method that enables a network to learn highly representative image features. We propose that using simple yet effective feature representations can outperform more complex meta-learning approaches. Experimental results on dermoscopic images demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method and show that even simple linear classifiers can achieve superior performance compared to established meta-learning methods.

Niobium is a prominent subject of research in the field of superconductors, 
encompassing both theoretical and experimental studies. Due to its significant 
importance in applications and its record-high superconducting transition 
temperature, $T_{c}=9.33$ K, niobium is utilized extensively for various uses, 
including power applications in alloys, magneto-sensing, radio-frequency 
cavities, and more recently, in the development of superconducting qubits. To 
improve the efficiency of these devices and reduce the loss of quantum coherence, 
a deeper understanding of niobium's electronic and superconducting properties, 
especially its anisotropies in the normal and superconducting states, is required. 
Recent research has proposed a microscopic theory to describe niobium's 
anisotropic properties in the presence of disorder. To validate this theory, 
we conducted an experiment where we exposed thin Nb films, produced under the 
same conditions as those used in transmon qubits, to 3.5 MeV proton irradiation. 
By measuring the superconducting transition temperature and upper critical fields, 
we demonstrated a distinct decrease in $T_{c}$ caused by potential (non-magnetic) 
scattering, which directly correlates with the anisotropic order parameter. The 
experimental results exhibit an impressive quantitative agreement with the 
theoretical predictions.

Public art displayed in urban areas can greatly influence community members' perceptions of belonging, as it often reflects the favored interests and cultural values of local power structures. A proposed system utilizes graph matching techniques with localized restrictions to create an interactive tool for selecting public art that fosters inclusivity. This method draws on Schelling's theory of segregation to generate a cost matrix, which is then used as input to solve an optimization problem through projected gradient descent. A soft assignment matrix is produced, allowing for flexible adjustments to curatorial constraints via added regularization terms. By optimizing artwork placement according to "in-group" depriortization criteria and adhering to exposure and representation requirements, the algorithm creates equitable distributions of public art. A developed fairness metric allows for assessment of the algorithm's output, with an actual test case conducted at Tufts University and considerations for potential drawbacks from a curatorial and equity standpoint.

Our comprehension of quantum mechanics in conjunction with gravity, essential for explaining numerous phenomena such as Hawking radiation and the early Universe's evolution, is limited by the unavailability of experiments that can reliably and feasibly probe quantum mechanics in curved spacetimes. To overcome this hurdle, we suggest an experiment involving a photon in a superposition state, splitting between two Sagnac interferometers of different diameters, thereby representing two disparate spacetimes. This setup enables us to predict the creation of entanglement even at low rotation speeds and demonstrates how the effects could be detected using Earth's rotation, thereby creating an accessible platform for investigating the spacetime's role in entanglement generation.

We analyze non-perturbative consequences of a specific deformation to the Mathieu differential equation, consistent with PT-symmetry, by establishing a connection between non-Hermitian and Hermitian scenarios. This is achieved through a reparameterization in the complex plane, followed by a restriction of the deformation parameter that preserves PT-symmetry in the Hermitian context. This factor appears in all non-perturbative outcomes and the transseries representation of the Mathieu partition function obtained. In quantum mechanics, the deformation parameter influences the real instanton solution for the Mathieu deformed potential in the Hermitian framework. As its value rises, the non-Hermiticity factor enables smoother instanton transitions, modifying the instanton width due to reduced potential barrier height. This effect persists for multi-instantons and instanton-anti-instanton pairs, where its equation of motion parallels the resistively shunted junction (RSJ) model.

The escalating air pollution crisis has prompted widespread concern globally, especially in the northern regions, where governments are launching large-scale monitoring systems to guide policy decisions. However, these initiatives are plagued by significant shortcomings: they are expensive, slow to implement, and biased towards urban areas, potentially exacerbating inequality. Furthermore, the process of estimating air pollution is often shrouded in opacity. This research showcases a groundbreaking method to estimate air pollution by leveraging publicly available data on road structures, focusing on England and Wales but with implications for global applicability. The innovative approach enables the creation of a low-cost, accurate air pollution estimation model that can be deployed across districts, providing transparent and explainable insights. We demonstrate the efficacy of a linear regression model utilizing a single structural property, achieving remarkable accuracy in pinpointing the most polluted districts within England and Wales. This model presents a game-changing alternative to expensive monitoring systems, offering practical value for policymakers seeking to advance clean-air initiatives without substantial investments. Its affordability, accessible design, and worldwide applicability create a foundation for implementing air pollution estimation systems in low-income countries.

Currently, vast amounts of Adaptive-Optics (AO) control data and telemetry are unavailable to end-users, but making them accessible has the potential to revolutionize the AO field, addressing various needs such as determining the system's PSF, characterizing turbulence, and optimizing system performance. To facilitate data sharing, we aim to overcome a major hurdle: the absence of standardization, which currently limits access. We propose developing a standardized, object-oriented Python package for AO telemetry that simplifies data access by utilizing a data model based on the Flexible Image Transport System (FITS), allowing for seamless integration with various AO systems, both existing and future, in their raw format or with detailed instrument information omitted. This package will be demonstrated using actual data from active AO systems at 10m-class observatories, with an initial focus on supporting the AOF and Keck systems, with further systems to be added.

This is the third installment of a series of works aimed at developing virtual structure sheaves and K-theoretic invariants in the context of moduli theory. Central to the investigation are almost perfect obstruction theories, a concept first proposed by Y.-H. Kiem and the author to facilitate the definition of K-theory invariants in relevant moduli stacks, including generalized K-theoretic Donaldson-Thomas invariants. The present study establishes virtual Riemann-Roch theorems in the framework of almost perfect obstruction theory for both non-equivariant and equivariant cases, encompassing cosection localized versions. This work builds upon and eliminates technical prerequisites introduced in the virtual Riemann-Roch theorems of Fantechi-G\"{o}ttsche and Ravi-Sreedhar. Key to the advancements are a comprehensive treatment of equivariant K-theory and Gysin maps of sheaf stacks, along with a formula for the virtual Todd class.

A key strategy in neuroscience research involves testing hypotheses using data from psychological and behavioral assessments, examining which factors - such as life events - contribute to certain outcomes, like depression.  Recently, deep learning has emerged as a potential method for analyzing these relationships by identifying key factors driving a specific outcome, yet its effectiveness has been hindered by the lack of a direct connection to the statistical relevance of the identified factors in confirming hypotheses.  In this study, we developed a versatile and scalable approach that combines hypothesis testing with data-driven deep learning analysis, using permutation testing to validate our results.  We applied our method to the annual self-reported evaluations of 621 adolescents in the National Consortium of Alcohol and Neurodevelopment in Adolescence (NCANDA), and found our approach could successfully determine the specific categories of risk factors associated with a symptom of major depressive disorder.

This article investigates the $L^{p}$-boundedness of pseudo-differential operators on a homogeneous tree, $\mathfrak{X}$. For a specific range of values, $1 < p < 2$, we examine how the $L^{p}$-boundedness on $\mathfrak{X}$ relates to that on the group of integers, $\mathbb{Z}$. We also derive an analogous form of the Calderon-Vaillancourt theorem for homogeneous trees, applicable to all values of $p$ excluding $2$.

We put forward a new fairness metric that loosens the strict equality requirements in the widely accepted equal odds fairness framework for classification tasks. A novel iterative approach, applicable to any model, employs a grid-based technique that ensures the predicted outcomes align with the metric for each sensitive attribute value individually. The method is capable of handling multiple values for a single attribute and performs a separate outcome sanitization process for distinct protected attribute values. Furthermore, we have adapted this approach to handle multiple attributes. By focusing on our target application of fraud detection, we demonstrate that the proposed method achieves fairness across multiple values of a single protected attribute and multiple protected attributes, while exhibiting comparable performance to existing fairness techniques that concentrate on two groups across several publicly available datasets.

This research introduces ThielSort, an efficient realization of the Diverting Fast Radix Algorithm.  Key theoretical advantages over traditional radix sort approaches are discussed, along with a detailed description of the implementation.  Experimental evaluation, encompassing a range of standard data distributions and input sizes, highlights the competitive performance of ThielSort with current top-tier algorithms.

To examine if the principle of entropy conservation remains consistent from the Big Bang's nuclear synthesis to the cosmic recombination, we consider the hypothetical decay of a massive particle into a combination of photons and other relativistic particles. Utilizing temperature and polarization fluctuations detected by Planck, spectral distortion limits set by COBE/FIRAS, and the measured abundance of primordial deuterium, we establish constraints for this hypothetical decay. The results indicate that if the decay particle's energy is distributed between 56% to 71% among photons, then its impact on the effective number of particles at recombination would be minimal, and Planck's data alone suggests a possible entropy increase. Additionally, our findings show that incorporating the bounds on primordial deuterium abundance enhances the constraints on the energy density of the decaying particle, which would be limited to a maximum contribution of 2.35% ($95\%$ CL) of the universe's total energy before it decays.

In our research, we explore Edgeworth expansions within the framework of limit theorems for self-normalized sums. By imposing minimal moment conditions, we establish non-uniform bounds for central limit theorem expansions. This achievement extends to non-integer moments, leading to an improved remainder. Furthermore, we provide non-uniform bounds for local limit theorems, which in turn facilitate the derivation of Edgeworth-type expansions and central limit theorems for self-normalized sums in the entropic central limit theorem and total variation distance.

Researchers in quantum thermodynamics have been trying to understand thermodynamic principles applied to machines functioning at the quantum level, where quantum properties like entanglement and coherence play a crucial role. Despite significant advancements, creating machines that showcase these effects has remained a challenge. In this study, the authors have conducted an experiment measuring the actual impact of quantum effects on thermodynamic principles. Using a single trapped ion qubit and manipulating it with laser pulses, they have implemented a quantum-based work protocol. The results from their two-time measurements showed that they align with a recently established quantum principle for work, contradicting classical expectations by more than ten standard deviations. The researchers also ruled out alternative explanations due to measurement errors by more than ten standard deviations. Furthermore, they found that the quantum correction disappears in extremely high temperatures, as predicted by theory.

This study examines minimal supersymmetric AdS$_3$ solutions on G$_2$-oriented backgrounds in type IIA and IIB supergravity, using the bispinor formalism to derive them. A straightforward case against AdS$_3$ solutions in massless type IIA string theory on such G$_2$ backgrounds is presented. Additionally, the research demonstrates that certain massive type IIA solutions allow for scale separation, in contrast to type IIB configurations, which do not. Furthermore, the paper derives a formula for the 3D superpotential in bispinor form applicable to both IIA and IIB configurations and shows that the supersymmetry conditions of this superpotential lead back to the bispinor equations.

In an upcoming series of lectures, we will delve into various probability laws governing the behavior of random points, curves, and surfaces. Starting with a brief introduction to martingales and one-dimensional Brownian motion, we will explore Bessel processes and their multivariate extensions, known as Dyson's Brownian motion model. We will then utilize Hilbert function spaces and Gaussian analytic functions to define and study determinantal and permanental-determinantal point processes. The Schramm-Loewner evolution and its complexification, which generates a family of conformally invariant probability laws of random curves, will also be a major topic of discussion. The final aspect of the lectures will focus on constructing and analyzing the behavior of multiple SLE curves, which can be established by coupling them with Dyson's Brownian motion model under specific conditions.

A general model of quadratic gravity and a single scalar field is analyzed to see how its gravitational degrees of freedom affect the parameters that describe the process of inflation. Our findings reveal that quantum corrections arising from a hypothetical particle known as the massive spin-2 ghost contribute substantially to the effective potential of inflation and enable the spontaneous breakdown of global scale invariance without requiring additional scalar fields. We calculate and compare the parameters that describe this model's inflation to those from well-established inflationary models and find that the predictions fit within the constraints set by the Planck and BICEP/Keck collaborations.

This paper aims to introduce a system within the Synthetic Data Vault for generating synthetic sequential data. A novel end-to-end framework, the Sequential model, has been designed and incorporated into SDV to build a generative model for multi-sequence real-world data. The system utilizes a unique neural network-based machine learning model, the conditional probabilistic auto-regressive model, which is available in the open-source SDV library alongside other models for diverse synthetic data requirements. We employed the Sequential SDV model to generate synthetic data and evaluated its performance by comparing it to a non-sequential generative adversarial network model, CTGAN. A custom metric, Multi-Sequence Aggregate Similarity (MSAS), was developed to assess the quality of the sequential synthetic data and verify that it retains higher-level patterns while matching the quality of real-world data.

Constraining physics models using maximum-likelihood estimation of observables is a crucial aspect of many experiments. To overcome challenges associated with small datasets and bounded parameters, the Profiled Feldman-Cousins method offers a viable solution for constructing precise confidence intervals, particularly when handling nuisance parameters effectively. This method provides superior frequentist coverage compared to other techniques, making it widely applicable to parameter estimation in neutrino oscillations and related measurements. An implementation of this method within the NOvA experiment is detailed here.

This study addresses the issue of minimizing energy in the presence of external influences on a spatially localized setting $X$, using a predefined kernel $\kappa$ that adheres to principles of energy and consistency. The research investigates the conditions under which $\lambda_{A,f}$ minimizes the given Gauss functional for a wide range of external fields $f$. This functional is evaluated across various measures of positive Radon $\mu$ concentrated within a defined region $A$, and these conditions are applied to provide a solution to a question raised by M. Ohtsuka in 1961. Specific results are presented for Riesz kernels $|x-y|^{\alpha-n}$ and illustrated through several examples. The study further provides alternative characterizations of $\lambda_{A,f}$ and examines its continuity under the exhaustion of $A$. The research yields new and applicable results for a wide variety of kernels in both classical and modern potential theory.

In recent years, convolutional neural networks have excelled in computer vision, leveraging their feature extraction capabilities and exceptional classification performance, as seen in the automated analysis of medical images like X-rays. However, these algorithms operate as "black boxes," making it challenging to comprehend their decision-making processes. To apply and evaluate such models across various fields, it is essential to employ eXplainable AI techniques. While medical research often focuses on binary or multiclass classification, many real-world scenarios, such as interpreting chest X-rays, involve multiple, co-occurring symptoms, which necessitate the use of multilabel classification. A significant limitation in these tasks is class imbalance, where different labels are represented by varying numbers of samples. This study presents a novel Deep Learning approach to addressing imbalanced, multilabel chest X-ray datasets, establishing a benchmark for the underutilized PadChest dataset and introducing a novel eXplainable AI method based on heatmaps, which incorporates probabilities and inter-model comparison. Our results demonstrate promising performance, particularly given the high number of labels used, and the generated heatmaps accurately identify areas relevant to expert decisions.

I'm investigating the dynamical instability of an ideal monatomic fluid in a framework of gravothermal evolution across various dimensions by applying Chandrasekhar's criterion to its quasistatic equilibria. When instability sets in, a collapse into a black hole may occur unless an external interaction halts the process. Notably, our three-dimensional spacetime is the optimal dimension where the fluid is stable but not overly stable. Moreover, this dimension supports stable hydrostatic equilibrium with a positive cosmological constant, whereas higher dimensions result in instability. Conversely, lower dimensions such as (2+1) lead to excessive stability. This analysis also touches on the role of negative cosmological constants in stabilizing fluid disks and supporting the cosmic censorship conjecture, which is further complicated by the possibility of emerging BTZ black holes with mass greater than zero. The significance of spacetime dimensionality is also briefly considered.

A highly advanced phase imaging technique called ptychography allows for non-invasive imaging at a nanometric level without causing any damage, and it's widely applied across various fields such as materials research and the defense sector. However, ptychography's main limitation lies in its time-consuming data collection process due to the need for high overlap between adjacent illumination areas to produce accurate reconstructions. This limitation arises from conventional approaches that utilize minimal overlap between scanning areas, which results in the inclusion of artifacts. This study introduces a novel solution by combining sparse, acquired data with data generated by a deep neural network to meet the sampling requirement in ptychography, thereby reducing experimental data collection time. We assess the method's effectiveness by comparing its reconstruction quality to that of established techniques and discuss the proposed method's benefits and drawbacks.

Maximizing the Gini index can result in suboptimal decisions due to a fundamental limitation. Specifically, the Gini index is a ranking-based metric that fails to account for calibration issues. Nonetheless, we demonstrate that consistency can be achieved when restricting to a specific class of calibrated regression models.

For infinitely numerous tensegrities and their variations, asymptotic equilibrium stresses are established, and a generalized form of the Roth-Whiteley rigidity definition is derived. Further, generalized versions of prestress stability and second-order rigidity are formulated for infinite frameworks composed of bars and joints, and it is demonstrated that these conditions are sufficient for continuous rigidity relative to bounded smooth motions. The underlying proofs rely on a newly developed concise proof for finite frameworks that prestress stability guarantees continuous rigidity.

This paper proposes Language Models as Data (LAD), a framework to generate high-quality synthetic dialogue data that captures essential structural patterns. By utilizing GPT-3 to foster linguistic diversity, LAD effectively supports the development of downstream dialog models. Results demonstrate notable improvements in zero-shot performance, with significant gains in intent prediction (+15%), slot filling (+31.4 F-1), and next action prediction (+11 F-1). Human evaluation confirms LAD's competitiveness with training on authentic human dialogue. Additionally, LAD's code and data are publicly accessible through https://github.com/Shikib/lad.

Consider a primitive character modulo a prime number $q$ and a positive value $\delta$. It has been noted that if the order of the character is high enough ($d \geq d_0(\delta)$), then there is at least one value $n$ less than or equal to $q^\delta$ for which $\chi(n)$ does not equal 1. We provide a new, simplified proof of this observation. Additionally, we show that if the order $d$ is squarefree and $d$ is large, then for any $d$th root of unity $\alpha$, the number of $n$ values up to $x$ such that $\chi(n) = \alpha$ is negligible compared to $x$ whenever $x$ is greater than $q^\delta$. As a result, we find that the values of $\{\chi(n)\}_{n \leq q^\delta}$ cannot cluster near 1 for any $\delta > 0$ when $\chi$ has sufficiently large order.

Our proof relies on a non-trivial second moment estimate for the characters $\chi^\ell$ on average over $1 \leq \ell \leq d-1$.
